book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
samples: Argues that the standard trio of moral failure - malice (Creed ogling Pam, Andy sabotaging Dwight with the toll-receipt trick), weakness of will (Jan returning to Michael, Meredith relapsing with alcohol), and ignorance (Pam trading away Jim's teapot in 'Christmas Party') - misses a fourth category: moral blindness, embodied by Michael Scott, who can recite moral rules but cannot see when they apply (his Martin Luther King name tag on Diversity Day, defending Phyllis from Todd Packer with a harassing kiss, the fake-firing prank on Pam). Against Plato's view that all wrongdoing is ignorance, the chapter claims knowledge of rules neither helps nor harms decency; what matters is moral perception - seeing what a situation requires - shown by Jim getting Dwight to the hospital and rescuing the Dundies, Pam protecting the Dwight-Angela secret, and Toby patiently answering Dwight's anatomy questions.

Weighs the morality of Jim and Pam's workplace flirting (while Pam is engaged to Roy) using three ethical frameworks: act utilitarianism has them tot up their own happiness against effects on co-workers' morale and Dunder-Mifflin's bottom line; rule utilitarianism models HR's blanket anti-dating policies and asks whether Jim and Pam could justify an exception without destroying the rule (the Hawaiian shirt day analogy); deontology searches for duties against office romance (favoritism in evaluation, distraction from duties) and finds none once harassment is set aside, concluding that in the absence of a deontological prohibition, Jim and Pam may keep flirting until 5 p.m.

Asks whether Michael can (not will) ever learn empathy, distinguishing cognitive empathy - explained via Russell's argument-by-analogy account of other minds, which Michael manages only with people like himself, hence his sales success in 'The Client' - from affective empathy, which he lacks (Kevin's possible skin cancer is 'terrible news for both of us'; he cannot read Phyllis's oven mitt in Yankee Swap). Traces his cluelessness to egocentrism, and following Hume and Smith's sentimentalist account of morals - decentring the ego toward the impartial spectator via emotional contagion - argues his only hope is a real friendship (Jim's) that could drag him outside himself, since sycophantic Dwight and one-sided Todd Packer never will.

Reads Tim Canterbury of the UK Wernham-Hogg as an autonomous moral agent who nonetheless cannot act on his own judgments: Kant's categorical imperative is applied to Tim's stapler-through-the-window prank (universalizing the maxim of disposing of disputed objects passes the test, so Tim is in the clear), before the chapter diagnoses the office's pointlessness with Durkheim, Fromm and Merton's notion of anomie - David Brent's management produces moral lawlessness and boredom. Tim's dice speech, his swallowed resignation and accepted promotion, and his last-second failed dash to Dawn in the finale show a weak-willed conscience: he knows what he should do but lacks the conviction, making him the moral conscience of the show without being its moral hero.

Uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of wit as a character virtue lying in a mean to map the UK office: David Brent is the buffoon of excess, the 'slave of his sense of humor' who cannot not joke (the 'crack of Dawn' line, the cruel Post-It Notes firing prank on Dawn), Gareth Keenan the boor of deficiency whose literalism leaves him unable to make or take a joke, and Tim Canterbury the ready wit whose responsive irony ('Does anybody have the right time?') hits the mean. Because humor, like morality, is uncodifiable - there is no Having a Sense of Humor for Dummies - the trio illustrates that virtue is qualitative appropriateness guided by practical wisdom, not moderation or rule-following.

Gives a crash course in epistemology (knowledge vs hypothesis, mistake, and opinion; empirical and rational evidence) to solve the puzzle of how Pam can simultaneously know and not know that she loves Jim: the evidence is public (Jim is 'onto' her, the teapot gift, Angela's 'Pam Pong' tally, her inspection of Jim's bedroom in 'Email Surveillance'), yet she tells the camera she and Jim are 'just friends' and angrily rejects the evidence (being picked up in 'The Fight', the 'first date' remark in 'The Client'). The chapter models self-deception as two kinds of knowledge plus an unjustified belief - she rationalizes the lie with genuine reasons (security with Roy, fear of losing control) until second-order knowledge of her own lying erupts as anger and despair, concluding the show is great because it is honest about the lies viewers tell themselves.

book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades
essays: When the Subject is Not the Butt Schmitts Gay Beer
Where in the Hell is Chris Rock
All Human Experience is an Impression
It’s Good to Be a Fan if …
We’re Here to Pump ‐clap‐ You Up! The Goal of SNL and “Weekend Update”
A New Holiday Album A Lesson Is in the Lyrics
That’s the News. Good Night and Have a Pleasant Tomorrow
Dysfunctional Family Feud The No Special Obligations View
samples: The editors introduce the volume by arguing that SNL, like philosophy, trains viewers to regard the world with a critical, questioning eye: four and a half decades of parody and satire wired generations of fans to think philosophically before they could articulate why. Land Shark, Spartan Cheerleaders, and Trump-era Update bits are cited as the shared generational memory the book will now analyze.

Tallman asks why SNL may mock presidents (Chase's pratfalling Ford, Carvey's Bush) and Clintons but not unchosen groups, framing the question with the aesthetics debate among radical autonomism (Bell), radical moralism (traced to Plato and Tolstoy), and moderate moralism. Sketches from Samurai Futaba to Farley's Lunchlady Land show jokes can punch up, punch down, or elevate a low-status group. The Schmitts Gay beer sketch, she argues, ridicules not gay men but beer-ad conventions: swapping the usual female sex objects for men in speedos exposes the objectification and heteronormativity viewers had stopped noticing, so the butt is the advertising industry.

Christiansen reads SNL's first head writer Michael O'Donoghue ('Mr. Mike') through Sartre: the Least-Loved Bedtime Tales (Brer Rabbit skinned alive, 'there's no moral... just random acts of meaningless violence') dramatize a world where existence precedes essence and narratives lie; 'Sartresky and Hutch' stages the absurd via a Vietnam veteran with PTSD; and the needles-in-the-eyes impressions embody Sartre's vulnerability to the Other, which Mr. Mike's dark glasses shut out. The chapter ends with Sartre's Marxist turn in the Critique of Dialectical Reason, arguing O'Donoghue's angry 'Police State' sketch shows that scarcity, alienation, and organized state violence are contingent and can be fought, which is where his nihilism leaves room for hope.

McGowan asks how SNL gets away with offensive material, from Larry David's concentration-camp monologue to the Chase-Pryor 'Word Association' and 'Nude Beach.' He argues censorship fails because offense is historically relative and slippery-slope prone, and that on Mill's On Liberty the harm principle never licenses suppressing speech SNL viewers can freely avoid, a point he sharpens with Feinberg's Volenti maxim and the offense principle. He closes by defending offensive comedy as robust social critique: Mill's fallibilist case that free speech drives human progress, with Baldwin's Trump and Tina Fey's Charlottesville bit as comedians speaking truth to power.

Reynolds places comedy on a spectrum from philosophy to satire to smart-assery and argues SNL mostly sits at the silly end: Gumby, Mr. Robinson, Hermione's cleavage, and Hobbit Office are parody with an absurd twist but no constructive target, unlike genuine satire such as Mr. Bill. He develops the comparison through Aristophanes' Clouds, whose caricature of Socrates at the Thinkery helped send him to his death, and through the 'Playboy Philosophy' sketch with Belushi as Socrates. Socrates himself emerges as a satirist: the oracle of Delphi, his claim to know only that he knows nothing, and his elenchus that unmasks the supposedly wise are read as comedy in the service of seriousness, before the chapter concedes SNL's absurdism is philosophical mainly in mocking an absurd world.

Irwin argues that SNL's caricatures (Fey's Palin, Baldwin's Trump, Aristophanes' Socrates in the Clouds) misrepresent their targets and that learning politics from comedy traps viewers in ideological bubbles, since satire flatters rather than informs. He introduces the Ideological Turing Test, adapted from Turing's test: state your opponent's view so accurately and sympathetically that a neutral observer cannot tell it is not yours, and grounds the duty to learn the other side from its own partisans in Mill's On Liberty. The 2016 'Bubble' sketch passes the test, he says, but SNL's liberal bias (gentle Sanders, untouchable Obama) rarely challenges its audience, and a conservative 'Live from Omaha' alternative would just rebuild the bubble on the other side.

book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
samples: The editor's Introduction explains why Spider-Man merits a philosophy book: Peter Parker is a self-reflective underdog with a strong moral compass he sometimes fails to follow, so his stories raise lived ethical questions rather than abstract metaphysics. Citing Plato's definition of philosophy as the love of wisdom and a way of life, Sanford frames the whole volume around Socrates' question 'how are you going to live your life?' and lists the questions Peter's life poses: the good life, the obligations attached to talents, friendship, identity over time, the ethics of enhancement, and whether life has meaning.

Mussett asks whether Peter Parker's painful life counts as a good life by testing five philosophers' answers against the comics and films. Kurtz's secular humanism finds Peter wanting in pleasure and acclaim (Uncle Ben dead by his inaction, J. Jonah Jameson's smear campaigns), while Rand's Objectivism condemns Spider-Man as the embodiment of the 'morality of sacrifice' she rejected, noting Steve Ditko's Objectivist devotion. Epictetus scores Peter highly on duty but fails him on self-mastery, since his happiness hinges on attachments to Aunt May and MJ he cannot control; Frankl would see Peter's meaning in his irreplaceable responsibility, evidenced by his refusal of Dr. Judas Traveller's offer of a peaceful life at the cost of innocents (Amazing Spider-Man #402); and Aquinas vindicates Peter's suffering as good pain in a virtuous, charitable life.

Kukkonen reads Peter's never-extinguished guilt over Uncle Ben as an 'infinite debt' modeled on Anselm's atonement theology: no good deed repays the primal transgression, so even the heroic serum rescue for Aunt May in 'The Final Chapter' (Amazing Spider-Man #33) leaves the debt intact. Against the Nietzschean escape into self-sufficient magnanimity (Ben's ghostly blessing in 'Doom Service!'), he argues via Levinas and Derrida that Peter's responsibility extends to every stranger, as when a rescued policeman with Uncle Ben's face calls him back in 'Spider-Man No More!' (#50). Following Kierkegaard's Works of Love, the chapter concludes that Peter's heroics do not pay off but deepen his debt of love, since every choice heeds one call while unavoidably failing others.

White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.

Barkman argues that Spider-Man's ethics, while universal enough for Jews, Platonists, and Confucians, are specifically Christian in emphasis: God creates for friendship, which requires free choice, so 'with great power comes great responsibility' restates Luke 12:48 — the more one is given, the more justice is required, as Peter's refusal of MJ and Octavius's wasted intelligence in Spider-Man 2 show. The free-will solution to the problem of evil (chosen evil, fallen angels, Adam's curse, a law-governed physical world) is read through Peter's questioning God in 'The Big Question' (Peter Parker: Spider-Man #48). The chapter culminates with Spider-Man 3, where the symbiote inflames Peter's grief into revenge against Sandman — a perversion of justice — until Peter forgives Flint Marko, enacting mercy as the perfection rather than the absence of justice.

Keeping asks what grounds the claim that great power brings great responsibility and answers through Good Samaritan ethics. Building on MacIntyre's account of human interdependence in family and community, and Mill's point that failing to aid can itself cause harm, he argues that Bad Samaritanism is a blameworthy harm-causing omission, so Spider-Man's rescues of strangers are obligatory negative duties rather than supererogatory favors. His vigilantism is excused because only he can stop supervillains, 'can implies ought' explains why his duties exceed ordinary people's, and his life-risking feats against the Sinister Six and Firelord still go beyond even what his enlarged duty demands.

book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
samples: Eberl reads Jax's Season 5 dilemma (Tara's ultimatum to leave SAMCRO or lose his family) through Aristotle's account of virtue as character cultivated by habituation in a polis. SAMCRO nurtures genuine virtues—Opie's selfless loyalty, courage under fire, the club's communal generosity toward Donna and Lyla—alongside vices like Clay's greed and Tig's lust, with the golden mean distinguishing Bobby's critical loyalty from Chuckie's obsequiousness and Juice's rash minefield charge. Fr. Ashby's fight to keep Abel in Belfast away from Jax's cycle of violence, and the contrast between Deputy Chief Hale's law-abiding ideals and Mayor Hale's self-serving development, illustrate Aristotle's claim that legislators and environments make citizens good or bad. The chapter concludes that Jax's very mix of virtue and vice—the 'savage' needed to head the table—may be what reform requires, at moral cost.

Uses Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals to explain why viewers root for SAMCRO's criminals: the Sons embody master morality, the warrior virtues of strength, boldness, and reverence for worthy enemies—seen in Jax's elaborate trap that gets Jimmy O killed and Opie executes Stahl in the Season 3 finale, and in Clay sparing Marcus Alvarez. Agent Stahl personifies ressentiment: after Otto disfigures her she vows 'I'm gonna bury these assholes,' dressing revenge as justice and respecting no one, while principled 'good guys' like Potter and Deputy Chief Hale internalize the slave morality of equality and sympathy. The lambs-and-birds-of-prey passage frames our unease at Jax dismissing Tig's murder of an unarmed woman as 'collateral damage,' and the chapter ends by weighing whether a world without noble 'blond beasts' like Jax would be Nietzsche's tragedy.

Takes Tig's misplaced revenge on Laroy—which kills Veronica Pope and triggers Damon Pope's burning of Tig's daughter and Opie's prison murder—together with the club's unconditional convoy rescue in 'To Be, Act 1' to ask whether loyalty is a virtue. It tests three accounts: the Aristotelian view (via Ladd's 'loyal Nazi is a contradiction') that only the virtuous can be loyal, which would deny that SAMCRO members can be loyal at all; the Humean view that loyalty is bigoted partiality; and the Kantian point that only the good will is unconditionally good, so loyalty can serve any wrongdoing. The chapter defends Ewin's line that loyalty is good in itself but issues in right action only joined with virtue, while the Stahl frame-up of Opie and Donna's death show the dark enforcement side—'rats deserve to die, end of story.'

Puts Aquinas's Murder Principle—the private, intentional killing of an innocent is always murder—to the Men of Mayhem, arguing the Sons lack the public authority Aquinas requires to kill even the guilty. The show itself erodes the state/private line Aquinas needs: corrupt agents Kohn and Stahl, and the CIA's Romeo Parada running the Galindo Cartel, make the badge look like no moral credential at all. The Doctrine of Double Effect sorts the rest: Jax shooting first in self-defense, Tara's morphine for the dying Unser, and Juice's hypothetical land-mine sacrifice are merely foreseen deaths, while Jax syringing Clay or Juice's intentional hanging would be murder. The chapter concludes that even if Aquinas condemns the Sons, his questions about authority, innocence, and intention are exactly the ones the show forces on viewers.

Reads John Teller's failed 'off the social grid' experiment through the human-nature debate: Mencius's seed of sympathy (even Tig recoils at Dante's dogfights) and Rousseau's naturally good man corrupted by society inspired J.T.'s Goldman-fed anarchism, while Mill and Xunzi counter that virtue is a victory over instinct. Hobbes supplies the real diagnosis—not innate violence but the logic of anarchy among free and equal rivals: competition (the Mayans blowing up the warehouse), diffidence (first-strike temptations against Zobelle), and glory (Jax unable to let the bike-sitting insult pass). Clay's rule that 'retaliation must be harsh and immediate' and the escalating Tig–Veronica Pope–Damon Pope–Opie bloodbath show deterrence fueling cycles of violence, so the only escape from the 'nasty, brutish, and short' fringe is the Leviathan's social grid.

Argues that a motorcycle club is a Machiavellian regime in miniature: Jax's Season 3 fake betrayal of the club to Stahl—actually a set-up that shortens the crew's prison time and delivers both Stahl and Jimmy O to death—shows the prince's union of lion and fox in service of the club rather than himself. J.T. figures as a founder overcome by fortuna ('each savage event was a catalyst for the next... blood was every color'), lacking the virtu to impose his vision, while Clay wields deceit and force for mere egoism that Machiavelli would refuse the name of glory. Zobelle's self-description as a 'Machiavellian fool' flooding Charming with drugs, and Jax's admission that 'you can't sit in this chair without being a savage,' frame the chapter's question of whether manipulation and violence can serve a genuine common good.

samples: The editors' introduction argues that South Park is one of TV's most important series because it lampoons the fanatical extremists of every social, ethical, economic, and religious position, modeling the fallibilist skepticism critical thinkers need (quoting Parker's line that the people screaming on both sides are the same and it is OK to laugh from the middle). It offers Peirce's account of thinking through incomplete signs and Derrida's 'play of differences' as case studies of this healthy skepticism, defends laughing at fanatics because their reasoning withers in sunlight, and previews the volume: Murtagh's 'sledgehammer' defense of blasphemous humor, Jacoby's Clifford-style case that belief without evidence is wrong, Dueck on rationally defensible faith, Gray on the 'Douche or Turd' election, and Held on gay marriage.

Young argues that South Park is perceived as dangerous for exactly the reasons Socrates was tried and executed in Plato's Apology: both 'corrupt the youth' by mocking religion, questioning authority, and exposing that the supposed teachers (Mr. Garrison's flip-flopping creationism, Mrs. Broflovski's moral panics, the 'Death' boycott of Terrance and Phillip) do not know what they think they know. He diagnoses Cartman as an Eichmann figure whose banal, thoughtless evil—feeding Scott Tenorman his parents, torturing Muslims with farts—consists in the inability to think from another's standpoint, while Kyle and Stan's friendship embodies Arendt's dialogic thinking and Aristotle's mean between ideological extremes, as when they see both the merit and the smugness of hybrid drivers in 'Smug Alert'. Freud's theory that jokes break through repression explains why the show's vulgarity is essential rather than gratuitous: it verbalizes what culture silences so that it can be thought through, making South Park a Socratic gadfly rather than a corrupter.

Jacoby defends W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief—it is wrong to believe on insufficient evidence and the burden of proof falls on the claimant—through Stan's exposures of TV psychic John Edward ('The Biggest Douche in the Universe'), the Scientology of 'Trapped in the Closet', and the faith-based story of Joseph Smith in 'All About Mormons'. The centerpiece is a South Park-illustrated demolition of Pascal's Wager: Kyle's hemorrhoid-driven despair in 'Cartmanland' shows a perfectly good God would not eternally reward evil Cartman or torture honest nonbelievers, and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' shows the wagerer cannot even know which religion pays out. Stan's closing speech to Edward's frightened audience carries the moral: comforting lies weaken the mind and slow the progress of finding the real, amazing answers.

Kirby reads the 'Imaginationland' trilogy as a satire of post-9/11 America interpreted through Ulrich Beck's world risk society: the Pentagon generals, still thinking in Cold War categories like 'Project X' and Chinese imagination portals, embody Beck's denial response and end up voting to nuke Imaginationland, while Cartman's Rambo-style self-interest embodies the apathetic response. Socrates' practice of demanding definitions frames the chapter's question of what terrorism actually is (via Hoffman's five criteria), and Socratic ignorance about what one does not know is contrasted with the worse condition of not being able to know what you do not know. Kyle's courtroom speech that imaginary beings like Luke Skywalker and Santa are 'realer' than most real people, and Butters' creative power to imagine Santa back to life, point to Beck's cosmopolitan 'transformation': imagination and cross-border cooperation as the way out of risk panic.

Arp uses the show as a logic textbook: his own prejudice against Goth kids and Officer Barbrady's post-Atlas Shrugged ban on books illustrate hasty generalization, Cartman's 'if you do drugs, then you're a hippie' chain and the Tooth Fairy syllogism illustrate deductive argument, and Towelie's appearances illustrate inductive strength. A fallacy catalog follows: Johnny Cochran's 'If Chewbacca lives on Endor, you must acquit' in 'Chef Aid' as red herring, Mrs. Broflovski's 'Death' boycott of Terrance and Phillip as slippery slope, Mrs. Marsh's cookie outburst in 'Clubhouses' as hasty generalization plus slippery slope, Father Maxi's hell pronouncements as appeal to inappropriate authority, and cartoon Rob Reiner in 'Butt Out' as ad hominem. The chapter's claim is that Parker and Stone deliberately violate logical principles episode after episode to expose absurd beliefs, because how people reason shapes the laws they make and the beliefs they die for.

Johnson uses 'Go God Go's' future of 2546—where Dawkins-style atheism has become a warring religion and otter scientists intone 'Oh my Science!'—to ask whether science and religion genuinely conflict and whether New Atheism is itself a faith. Applying abduction and the four criteria of adequacy, he argues the embellished-story hypothesis beats miracle claims about Jesus (whose legend grew Gospel by Gospel), Sathya Sai Baba, Joseph Smith, and Xenu, that Mr(s). Garrison's 'you can't disprove God' and the show's sarcasm commit an appeal to ignorance, and that Stan's water-into-wine scene with Jesus shows how easily people are fooled. He allows Kuhnian theory change in science but rejects James's will-to-believe for existence claims—the moon whale Willzyx needs evidence—and concludes Parker and Stone are unfair to Dawkins: ending religion would not end violence, but it would remove the easiest justification for it, and some answers are simply true even when unknown.

book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
samples: Editors Decker and Eberl open with William Shatner's 1986 'Get a life' Saturday Night Live skit and argue that thousands of hours spent watching Star Trek are not wasted, because the show is a treasure trove of philosophical questions. They preview the volume's ethics chapters on captains' moral psychology and the Prime Directive (asking why Kirk is so hellbent on destroying utopian civilizations), its social-political chapters on Klingons, Borg values, Federation economics versus Ferengi capitalism, and justice in the Q Continuum, and its metaphysical chapters on whether Data and Voyager's holographic Doctor are persons, Riker's duplication, and holodeck skepticism. It closes by framing Roddenberry's secular humanism against the seriously treated religious cultures of the Klingons and Bajorans.

Jason Eberl uses the amusement park of 'Shore Leave', Omicron Ceti III's spore paradise in 'This Side of Paradise', Landru's hedonistic 'red hour', and the Borg's relentless efficiency to argue that edifying play and leisure are necessary for intellectual, moral, and spiritual flourishing. Following Josef Pieper's Leisure, with Nozick's experience machine (applied to 'The Thaw' and Barclay's holodiction), Aristotle's 'we work in order to be at leisure', and Aquinas on wonder, he contrasts mere utility (bonum utile) with the common good a drone-only Collective can never have. He concludes that thoughtfully watching Star Trek is itself worthwhile leisure: science-fiction thought experiments that serve Socrates's examined life.

Jerold Abrams reads J. J. Abrams's Kirk as Aristotle's megalopsychos and 'god among men' from the Politics: too excellent to be a mere crewmember, disdainful of rank, speaking openly from love and hate, and a law unto himself. The four-on-one bar fight, reprogramming the unwinnable Kobayashi Maru, declaring 'Some should be' above the Prime Directive to Pike, and his exile to frozen Delta Vega (like the Argonauts stranding Heracles) all enact Aristotle's dilemma that a society must either exile such a man or submit to his monarchy. Spock, a great-souled man himself, becomes Kirk's 'second self' in Aristotle's truest friendship once Kirk takes the captain's chair.

Tim Challans treats Kirk, Picard, Archer, and Janeway as case studies in moral psychology, with the captain as Plato's charioteer balancing the horses of Spock's logic and McCoy's feeling. He reads Picard's 'there are four lights' coercion in 'Chain of Command' and his Locutus guilt in 'Family' through Rawls's shame/guilt distinction and Nancy Sherman's 'moral injury', while Kirk's 'I need my pain' refusal of Sybok and Archer's Xindi-era regrets show commanders owning guilt, regret, and remorse. Drawing on Nussbaum's 'upheavals of thought' and Hume's passions, he argues that a rare, well-integrated moral psychology—pride tempered by humility, as Q's lesson in 'Tapestry' demonstrates—is what qualifies the one-in-a-million starship captain.

Barcenas and Bein pit Kant against Confucius on the Prime Directive, opening with Kirk's Nibiru volcano rescue of Spock in Into Darkness. Kant's categorical imperative—universalization and respect tests applied to Scotty's dilemma in 'Bread and Circuses' and Worf's 'not a matter of degree'—makes the Directive absolute, while Confucius and Aristotle ground morality in cultivated character: a junzi like Picard may bend the rule when virtue demands it, as in 'Pen Pals' and rescuing Wesley from the Edo in 'Justice'. They conclude Starfleet needs both: the Kantian rule for most officers, and exemplary persons like Picard to know when the rule fails.

David Kyle Johnson argues Kirk is a jerk for dismantling utopias—the machine-god Vaal in 'The Apple' and the spore colonists of Omicron Ceti III in 'This Side of Paradise'—whose members were happy, healthy, and arguably free. Taking up objections from the Mission Log podcast, he rebuts the 'stagnation' and 'drug' charges by testing the utopias against Aristotle's eudaimonia and Maslow's self-actualization, and exposes the appeal-to-nature fallacy behind 'artificial happiness'. Using Rousseau on primitive simplicity and Nozick's libertarian minimal state, he concludes that the real threat to freedom is Kirk himself (and a Federation that, as Eddington says, assimilates without telling you), and that at minimum cultural relativism forbids wrecking harmless societies.

book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
samples: The editors frame the volume through fan controversies (Han or Greedo, Jar Jar, the de-canonized Expanded Universe) and the philosophical question each film raises, from whether a prophesied destiny robs Anakin of freedom to whether good and evil are mere 'points of view.' They invoke Hegel's claim that philosophy captures only its own time to concede this 'ultimate' volume predates Episode VII. The introduction connects Star Wars to philosophy by previewing the essays: Stoic Jedi, the Sith's Thrasymachus-like worldview, Boba Fett's amoralism, feminist readings of Padme and Leia, Kevin Smith's charge that the Rebels are terrorists, Joseph Campbell's monomyth, droid minds, and whether Chewie can speak.

MacMullan argues Darth Plagueis is a paradox for Plato: wisdom as reason ruling spirit and appetite should be impossible for a Sith who feeds on passion, yet Plagueis stays patient, restrained, and rational for over a century. He reads Sidious's 'I will make it legal' and the Sith Code as Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger,' and notes Plagueis even shares Plato's noble lie and eugenic breeding programs. Finding that Plato's prediction of self-destruction fails for Plagueis, the chapter turns to Nietzsche: master morality, the will to power, and life beyond good and evil better explain a Sith who cherishes bodily life and seeks to conquer death where Yoda and Socrates calmly disdain 'crude matter.'

Hummel maps the Jedi Order onto Epictetus's Stoicism: philosophy as a way of life, virtue through wisdom, the dichotomy of control ('some things are up to us'), and treating outcomes like flying or other people's fates as preferred indifferents within the will of the Force. Anakin falls because he misconceives power as the ability to do amazing things - stopping people from dying - instead of mastery of his own judgments, and he refuses Stoic indifference toward Shmi and Padme. The chapter also indicts the Jedi's own un-Stoic lapses: mind tricks on Watto, entering the Clone Wars, and Mace Windu's attempt to execute a subdued Sidious.

Lindenmuth reads Luke's endgame in Return of the Jedi as Kierkegaard's knight of faith, reversing Abraham's binding of Isaac: where Abraham raised the knife, Luke, pressed by Yoda and Obi-Wan to kill his father, throws his saber away. Jedi detachment ('train yourself to let go') is infinite resignation, and Han Solo's arc from self-interested smuggler to hero at Yavin traces Kierkegaard's aesthetic-to-ethical stages. Luke's double movement - resigning everything, his cause and his life, while trusting there is still good in Vader - suspends the ethical demand to kill and accomplishes what neither side thought possible: turning a Sith back to the light.

Adams pairs Anakin with Achilles to show how Palpatine's lesson that 'good is a point of view' - Nietzsche's claim that there are no moral facts, only interpretations - nearly destroys both heroes before a father's love pulls them back: Priam's tears before Achilles, Luke unmasking Vader. Against nihilism the chapter defends moral realism through Apollo's lion simile (compassion and respect are objective facts about what persons require) and Kant's self-critical inquiry, with the Jedi Council's twelve-way deliberation illustrating that some interpretations are better than others, beyond Hume's problem of induction. Both epics settle on a 'Pagan Golden Rule' - help your friends and harm your enemies, but never lose compassion for either.

Decker parallels the Republic's fall into Palpatine's Empire with the Zhou dynasty's collapse that birthed Chinese philosophy, reading three Jedi from the Dark Times comics through it. K'Kruhk, guided by the Zatoichi-like Master Zao, learns wu-wei - following the Force rather than forcing outcomes, with Laozi's Dao as the Force's Chinese analogue. Dass Jennir's struggle over what 'Jedi' means after killing a slaver becomes Confucian rectification of names and the cultivation of ren, while Kai Hudorra's loss of faith, withdrawal to a casino, and final sacrificial stand against Vader embody Mozi-style pragmatic minimalism redeemed by Jennir's virtuous example.

book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
essays: Jedi and Sith Ethics “Similar in Almost Every Way”
A New Hope Inclusive Representation in the Galaxy
“We Were Trained to Be Keepers of the Peace, not Soldiers”
Do Not Ask Him to Be Rational
Trust in the Force of Others
“You Like Me because I'm a Scoundrel”
“An Energy Field Created by All Living Things”
“Master Skywalker. There Are Too Many of Them. What Are We Going to Do ”
samples: Editors Eberl and Decker explain why this follow-up to their 2005 Star Wars and Philosophy volume is organized chronologically across the films, The Clone Wars, Rebels, The Bad Batch, Rogue One, Solo, and The Mandalorian. They situate the book against Disney's 2012 canon reset, the TV revival, and the 'Fandom Menace' backlash against diverse casting, arguing Star Wars holds a mirror up to the culture wars. The introduction previews the volume's questions, from natural law and the ethics of the Force to droid love, hope in dark times, and whether you should eat Baby Yoda.

Johnson reads The Phantom Menace as having distinctly Daoist flavors: Shmi's 'you cannot stop the change any more than you can stop the suns from setting,' the Naboo-Gungan 'symbiont circle,' and midi-chlorian symbiosis all express the Daoist unity of opposites and the constant flow of change. He argues Qui-Gon Jinn acts as a Daoist sage practicing wu wei — 'concentrate on the moment,' 'another solution will present itself' — while nearly everyone else in the film makes wrong predictions and grasps at outcomes. Even Anakin's accidental 'Oops!' victory over the Droid Control Ship is presented as success without trying, the practical meaning of 'Do or do not. There is no try.'

Harter argues that Revenge of the Sith manipulates audiences into fearing the medical technology that saves Anakin on Mustafar, portraying his prosthetic transformation into Vader as horrifying when in real bioethical terms saving a burn victim with ventilators, feeding tubes, and prosthetics is something we applaud. He diagnoses Lucas's framing as the naturalistic fallacy (what is natural is good), grounded in Hume's is-ought gap, and flags the mirror-image 'technological fallacy' of assuming enhancement like General Grievous's cyborg body must be good. The chapter concludes that technology is value-neutral and its worth depends on the context of use — which is what it means for Anakin and Luke, both maimed and prosthetized, to 'bring balance to the Force.'

Shea, Archer, and Banning argue that Star Wars' moral framework is natural law ethics in the tradition of Aristotle and Aquinas: the light side humanizes (Force healing, Qui-Gon's spirit surviving death, Grogu curing Greef Karga) while the dark side dehumanizes (Maul's bisection, Palpatine's deformation, Anakin's disfigurement), and apparent counterexamples like Luke's lost hand always trace back to prior vice. Aquinas's claim that the most general principles of natural law can never be blotted out explains why 'there is still good in' Vader and why redemption is always possible. The Jedi and Sith codes embody opposed views of human nature — relational, altruistic, and accepting of mortality versus atomistic, egoistic, and obsessed with cheating death through midi-chlorian manipulation.

Lakka uses Beauvoir's The Second Sex (the Mother/Mistress dichotomy, woman tied to nature and denied transcendence) and Butler on the mother-daughter separation to argue that Revenge of the Sith reduces Padme from the active senator and warrior of the first two prequels to a pregnant figure confined to her apartment, whose death gets read as martyrdom or even 'mom-shaming.' She reads Anakin's jealousy, interrogations ('Obi-Wan's been here, has he not?'), and Force-choke on Mustafar — explicitly paralleled with Othello and Desdemona — as an abusive relationship, suggesting Padme's death may be a feminicide. The deleted Petition of the 2000 scenes, and successors like Rey, Ahsoka, Rose Tico, and Jyn Erso, point toward the inclusive representation the galaxy still needs.

Challans reads the clone army as a Foucauldian project of discipline: Kaminoan reconditioning, punishment of 'aberrance,' and the inhibitor chips produce the 'docile bodies' that made Order 66 executable, with Palpatine's propaganda framing the Jedi as traitors to supply its legitimacy. Milgram's obedience experiments explain why most clones became 'agentic' executioners, while the rare independence of Rex, Fives, and Tup in the Umbara arc — 'we are not a bunch of unthinking droids!' — shows how fragile moral autonomy is. He concludes that military competence itself requires independent judgment, as his Delta Force versus Rangers comparison after Mogadishu illustrates, making Rex the exemplar of the moral autonomy the chips were designed to destroy.

book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
essays: 1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone
samples: The editor's introduction argues that the fans' endless Batman-vs-Superman fight is never really about who is stronger or richer but about who is the better hero — who we should try to be like, raise our children to resemble, and model our future on. Recalling learning sacrifice from Batman and total self-giving from the Death of Superman storyline, it frames the book's debate format as a choice between hopeful faith that humanity will succeed and cynical suspicion that everyone is one lab accident from villainy, and hands the verdict to the reader.

Holdier tests each hero against Nietzsche: Superman looks like the Übermensch but his mild-mannered Clark Kent pose is slave morality that would turn Nietzsche's stomach, while Batman's will-forged heroism (his Year One vow, 'what does not kill me makes me stronger') seems more overman-like until his self-loathing in Hush ('deep down, I'm not [a good person]') disqualifies him too. Neither qualifies; instead Superman embodies the Apollonian sun-god force of The Birth of Tragedy and Batman the Dionysian, so their Dark Knight Returns clash is the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles — and the readers are the ones who win the fight.

Alloy uses the problem of political obligation to split the heroes: against Plato's Crito, where Socrates refuses escape because even bad laws bind, Bruce Wayne simply flees arrest in Bruce Wayne: Murderer?/Fugitive, treating law as a tool of his war. He tests consent theory through Superman's chosen handcuffs in Man of Steel and Darkseid's Apokolips as Hobbes's 'mortal god' versus Locke's natural-rights standard, lets Hume's objection sink tacit consent (Red Son Superman cannot really emigrate, and Batman would never leave Gotham), rejects gratitude theory via the Kents' adoption of Kal-El, and dismantles Batman's 'I'm not wearing hockey pads' defense with Nozick's Batman-lottery — concluding Superman's law-conforming restraint protects the public from him becoming Luthor's 'alien overlord', while answerable-to-no-one Batman remains a force of chaos.

Springett applies evolutionary biology to the debate: natural selection, fitness (Batman edges it by one child, Damian Wayne), morphospace reasoning, and biological altruism, which technically Batman satisfies better since invulnerable Superman cannot lower his own fitness. But judged as an effective helper at species scale — Gould's catastrophes, asteroids, alien invasions — Superman protects the fitness of the whole species and planet where Batman guards one city, so a closing three-premise argument crowns Superman the superior Superhero, and his habit of saving the less fit makes him a living counterexample to Social Darwinism.

Farrell traces the heroes to medieval knighthood and evaluates them by C.S. Lewis's 'The Necessity of Chivalry': both live the double demand of fierceness and meekness (Batman brutalizing the Joker in The Dark Knight yet gifting a boy his surveillance gear; Superman turning back time for Lois yet rescuing a girl's cat), and both must achieve knightly character 'by art, not nature'. The decisive difference is restraint: Superman's Pa Kent lessons and the Smallville 'Red' red-kryptonite episode show the mighty man choosing self-control, making Kal-El the truer chivalric knight, where Lewis's examples (Achilles, triumphant generals) show power without meekness is no heroism.

LaBauve opens with an imagined Justice League showdown over a Joker hostage where Batman sways the crowd with pathos (fear of failing the innocent) and Superman wins them back through ethos — years of trusted character — to stage the chapter's claim from Aristotle's On Rhetoric. Superman alone balances all three appeals: Batman's pathos is all too human (Nolan's tormented Bruce) and his logos is master-detective method, but pure pathos risks Hitler-style demagoguery and pure logos is inhuman, while Superman's surpassing ethos — reinforced by the Kill Bill Vol. 2 monologue that Clark Kent is the costume — makes him the virtuous exemplar who 'must win'.

book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
samples: Written in the voice of the GhostFacers mourning their slain intern Alan Corbett, the introduction presents the volume as their covert infiltration of 'the industry of philosophy.' It reports that philosophy derives from the Greek philosophia, 'loving wisdom,' and jokes that the philosophers it recruited all 'readily admitted that they knew nothing' yet kept pursuing it, with a running gag about whether knowledge itself might be a tulpa. It frames the following essays as the GhostFacers' manifesto of truth about what exists in the Supernatural universe, ghosts and demons included and the Winchester 'Wine-chesters' excluded.

Nathan Stout uses P.F. Strawson's account of moral responsibility through 'reactive attitudes' to ask when Sam and Dean are justified in killing what they hunt. Monsters sort into three groups: low-functioning animal killers like the wendigo and 'Heart''s werewolf Madison, intelligent but conscienceless 'antisocial' monsters like demons and leviathans, and 'moral monsters' like the cow-blood-drinking vampires of 'Bloodlust' and the kitsune Amy from 'The Girl Next Door,' who can understand and be motivated by moral reasons. Because Group 3 monsters are members of the moral community, Dean's 'if it's supernatural, we kill it' bigotry and his secret killing of Amy make the supposedly good hunters morally suspect, since killing a fellow member of the moral community ought to weigh on them.

Foresman and Tobienne deploy Aristotle's apparatus of essence and accident, the ten categories, and actuality versus potentiality to define the monster and explain the show's appeal. They test candidates against canon: whether hunting is essential or accidental to Sam after Azazel's kills, what John Winchester in 'Dead Man's Blood' treats as essential to vampire substance, and Madison's transformation in 'Heart' from actual human and potential werewolf into actual monster, concluding that monstrosity lies in thought and action rather than appearance, as the human-hunting but human Benders confirm. Tracing 'monster' to the Latin monstrum, a sign or omen, they argue monsters are monsters only through their relation to human self-importance, so our 'speciesist' prejudice is exactly why we love watching them hunted, and why we love Supernatural.

Shannon Ford reconstructs the Winchesters' ethics of killing: self-defense and defense of others justify lethal force, as when Sam kills Jeremy in 'Dream a Little Dream of Me' and Andy shoots Ansem to save Dean in 'Simon Said,' while Dean's refusal of Ruby's virgin-sacrifice spell in 'Jus in Bello' and sparing the disarmed Pa Bender mark lines they will not cross even when the math favors killing. Killing possessed innocents like Meg is treated as permissible only under necessity and with regret. The chapter then argues that once the brothers hunt to banish all demons from the world, their conflict is war rather than hunting, so just war theory (jus ad bellum and jus in bello) might license killings ordinary morality forbids, a slippage dramatized by Gordon's enjoyment of killing and Dean's unjustifiable killing of Amy.

Ralston and Applegate read the Winchesters' contested destiny through the free will debate: the angels' case for determinism runs from a cupid arranged to couple John and Mary, through Azazel's deal and Mary's death, to Zachariah and Michael's claim that 'free will is an illusion' and the brothers must say yes as vessels. Sartre supplies the response: with no pre-given essence, the Winchesters are radically free and responsible, Dean admirably resisting 'bad faith' while Sam's early rebellions are self-deceptive until he stops blaming family expectations. Hume's point that free choices must still flow from the agent's character and values grounds a two-stage model of free will used to argue that soulless Sam, lacking the moral filter of the soul, has more options but is less free and less responsible.

Foresman asks what would make Hell a justified punishment for the souls claimed by crossroads deals, like Mary, John, and Dean trading damnation to bring a loved one back to life. Using Joel Feinberg's expressive account of punishment, he argues that souls in Hell through stupid deals suffer mere bad consequences rather than punishment, because no message of moral condemnation reaches someone who never knew the rule. Bentham's utilitarian test fails to justify Hell, since a Hell nobody takes seriously deters nobody and nothing there is rehabilitated, and Kantian retributivism fails too because no finite wrong can deserve eternal torment, leaving Crowley's endless-queue Hell as at least better proportioned to desert.
